description: How rulers and cities used myth to project power — from the Parthenon sculptures to the imagery of Augustus.
content_html:
Myth as a Political Language

In the ancient world, myth was not merely entertainment. The myths chosen for public display in temples, on friezes, on altars and in statues carried deliberate political messages. When a ruler or a city chose to depict a particular battle between gods and monsters, or a hero defeating savagery, they were making a statement about themselves: we are the forces of order, civilisation and divine favour; our enemies are chaos and barbarism. Understanding how myth was used to express power requires reading ancient art not just aesthetically but politically — asking not only “what does this show?” but “why was this chosen, and what did it communicate to its audience?”

The Centauromachy on the Parthenon

The Parthenon in Athens, completed in 438 BC, was the most spectacular expression of Athenian power and pride. Its sculptures were designed as an integrated programme of mythological messaging. On the metopes — the carved panels between the triglyphs on the exterior of the temple — the south side depicted the Centauromachy: the battle between the Lapiths (a Greek people) and the Centaurs. The story was that the Centaurs had been invited to a wedding feast and, drunk on wine, attacked the Lapith women and attempted to carry them off. In the marble metopes, the conflict is shown in vivid, energetic relief: each panel shows a single combat between a Lapith and a Centaur, muscles straining, limbs entwined, the victory of civilised form over bestial violence. The Centaurs are wild and ungainly; the Lapiths are controlled and graceful even in struggle.

The message was transparent to any educated Greek viewer: the Lapiths represented Athens and the Greeks; the Centaurs represented the Persians, who had invaded Greece in 480–479 BC and been driven back by Athenian courage. This mythological allegory allowed the Athenians to celebrate their military victory in religious, universal terms: we did not merely defeat invaders, we defeated barbarism itself.

Key Fact

The south metopes of the Parthenon show the Centauromachy. Each of the thirty-two panels (originally) showed a single combat between a Lapith and a Centaur. The choice of this myth was deliberate: Centaurs represented barbarism and disorder; Lapiths represented Greek civilisation. The parallel with the Persian Wars was clear to every Athenian who approached the temple.

The Amazonomachy on the Bassae Frieze

The Temple of Apollo at Bassae (in the Peloponnese) had a continuous interior frieze — now in the British Museum — depicting two battles: a Amazonomachy (Greeks fighting the Amazons) and a Centauromachy. The Bassae frieze, carved in the late fifth century BC, is remarkable for its dynamic composition: figures pile on top of one another, weapons clash, Amazons in exotic eastern costumes fight Greek heroes. The Amazon myth was particularly rich in political symbolism. The Amazons were a race of warrior women from the east — their very existence violated Greek social norms (women who fought, who rejected men, who came from the barbaric east). Defeating them in myth meant defeating the “other” in the most complete possible sense: not just a foreign people, but a foreign way of ordering the world.

Both the Centauromachy and the Amazonomachy served the same political-mythological function: they mapped Greek victory over a monstrous or barbaric “other” onto the Greek experience of the Persian Wars. The Centaurs and the Amazons were both perceived as threats to the Greek social order — Centaurs represented uncontrolled animal appetite; Amazons represented a world with the sexes inverted. By showing Greek heroes defeating these mythological enemies, the art celebrated not just military power but the rightness of the Greek way of life. It also worked religiously: these battles took place on sacred buildings dedicated to the gods, implying divine approval of the Greek cause. The gods themselves endorsed the defeat of chaos.

Augustus and the Use of Myth

No ruler of the ancient world used myth more systematically as a tool of political power than Augustus, the first Roman emperor. After the chaos of the civil wars that destroyed the Roman Republic, Augustus presented himself as the restorer of peace and order — and he anchored that claim in myth and religion. He rebuilt temples, revived ancient rituals and embedded himself in Rome’s divine mythology at every opportunity.

The Augustus of Prima Porta statue communicates his power through layered mythological reference. Augustus stands in the pose of a Roman commander, his arm extended as if addressing troops. His breastplate (cuirass) is covered with carved scenes: at the centre, a Parthian commander returning Roman military standards to a Roman general — a real diplomatic triumph of 20 BC that Augustus used as propaganda. Above this scene the sky god (Caelus) holds out his canopy of stars; below sits the earth goddess (Terra), surrounded by symbols of plenty. Sol (the sun) and Aurora (the dawn) drive their chariots at the sides. The whole breastplate presents the Roman world as cosmically ordered under Augustus’s leadership. At the base of the statue, Cupid rides a dolphin — a clear reference to Augustus’s claimed descent through Julius Caesar to Aeneas and then to Venus herself. The statue does not just show a soldier; it shows a man whose rule is woven into the fabric of the universe.

Key Fact

The Augustus of Prima Porta statue (Vatican Museum) is the supreme example of Roman myth used as political propaganda: the breastplate cosmogram, the Cupid dolphin reference to Venus, and the oratorical pose all work together to present Augustus as divinely sanctioned ruler of a cosmically ordered empire.

The Ara Pacis of Augustus

The Ara Pacis (Altar of Augustan Peace), dedicated in 9 BC, was a marble altar enclosed within carved walls. The monument worked on two levels simultaneously. At the literal level, it celebrated a real event: Augustus’s return from successful campaigns in Spain and Gaul in 13 BC, and the peace he brought. At the mythological level, its relief panels embedded this peace in a divine narrative. One panel showed Aeneas making a sacrifice — the ancestor of Rome, the Trojan hero, performing the same pious act of thanksgiving that Augustus was now repeating, showing Roman history as one long sacred covenant between the people and the gods. Another panel showed the goddess Roma seated in armour on a throne of captured weapons, serene and powerful. A third showed a mother goddess (possibly Pax, goddess of peace, or Venus) seated with abundant natural gifts around her — children, animals, flowing water and grain. The overall message: peace, fertility, divine blessing and cosmic order had all arrived with Augustus.

Both Greek and Roman uses of myth for political purposes share the same basic logic: myth gives events a cosmic, divine frame that makes them seem inevitable and approved by the gods. But there are important differences. Greek mythological allegory (the Parthenon Centauromachy; the Bassae Amazonomachy) tended to be indirect — it did not show Athenians fighting Persians directly but encoded the message in mythological form. Roman uses of myth under Augustus were often more direct and personal: the Augustus of Prima Porta puts the emperor himself at the centre of the mythological cosmos; the Ara Pacis shows his family in procession alongside mythological allegories. The Roman emperor was the link between the divine world and the human world in a way no Athenian democratic politician could ever be.
exam_tip_html: Questions on myth as a symbol of power will often ask you to analyse a specific source — a description of the Parthenon metopes, the Bassae frieze, the Augustus of Prima Porta, or the Ara Pacis. The key analytical move is always to ask: what is being shown, and what political message does it send? For the Greek examples, connect the mythological battles (Centauromachy, Amazonomachy) to the Persian Wars and the idea that the “other” represents barbarism. For the Roman examples, show how Augustus embedded himself personally in a divine narrative (divine descent via Aeneas and Venus; Cupid on the Prima Porta statue; Aeneas sacrificing on the Ara Pacis). Never simply describe a source — always explain the ‘why’: why was this myth chosen, and what did it make an audience believe?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Myth was a political language in the ancient world: the Centauromachy on the Parthenon south metopes and the Amazonomachy on the Bassae frieze both used mythological battles to celebrate Greek military victory (especially over the Persians) as the triumph of civilisation over barbarism.
  • Augustus used myth more personally and directly: the Augustus of Prima Porta breastplate presents the emperor at the centre of cosmic order, while the Ara Pacis links his reign to Aeneas’s piety and Rome’s divine destiny.
  • In both cultures, the key question to ask is not just “what does this show?” but “why was this myth chosen here, on this building, for this audience?” — the location and context of mythological art is always part of its meaning.

practice_questions.text: Name the mythological battle shown on the south metopes of the Parthenon.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Centauromachy (the battle between the Lapiths and the Centaurs).

practice_questions.text: Describe the Ara Pacis and explain its purpose.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate details: it is a marble altar (and enclosing walls) in Rome; it was dedicated in 9 BC; it celebrated Augustus's return from campaigns in Spain and Gaul; its panels show a procession of the imperial family; mythological panels include Aeneas sacrificing; a panel shows the goddess Roma; a mother-goddess panel celebrates fertility and peace; it connected Augustus's reign to Rome's divine destiny.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following description of a decorated surface on a famous Greek temple:

Across the outer wall of the building, a series of carved panels showed individual combats between civilised men and monstrous creatures that were part-human, part-horse. In each scene the human fighters are shown with controlled, graceful bodies, while their opponents are wild and ungainly. The scenes were carved at the highest level of the building, visible to all who approached.

Using the passage and your own knowledge, explain what these carvings communicated to people who saw them in the fifth century BC.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Analyses at least three elements of the source with precise own-knowledge support. Identifies this as the Centauromachy on the Parthenon south metopes; explains the deliberate contrast (controlled/graceful Lapiths vs wild/ungainly Centaurs = Greek civilisation vs barbarian chaos); links to the Persian Wars allegory (Lapiths = Athenians / Greeks; Centaurs = Persians/barbarians); notes the placement at the top of the building (visible to all, religious context = divine sanction); connects to the broader programme of Parthenon sculpture (east pediment birth of Athena; west pediment Athena–Poseidon; Panathenaic frieze). Evaluates what the choice of this myth communicated about Athenian power and identity.
Secure (4): Analyses two elements with clear explanation; names Parthenon and the Persian Wars connection.
Developing (3): Identifies one or two details; some explanation; may be mainly descriptive.
Emerging (1–2): General comments with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Augustus of Prima Porta statue uses myth and divine imagery to reinforce Augustus's power.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the statue (marble statue, Vatican Museum, found at Prima Porta); 1 mark for one specific mythological/divine detail explained (Cupid on dolphin = divine descent through Venus; breastplate cosmos = Augustus at the centre of divine order; the Parthian standards scene = military triumph framed cosmically); 1 mark for a second specific element explained; 1 mark for an overall conclusion connecting the imagery to the political claim Augustus was making (his rule = divinely ordained, cosmically inevitable).

practice_questions.text: How effectively did the Greeks and Romans use myth to express and reinforce political power? Use a range of named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained argument covering both cultures and evaluating effectiveness. Greek: Parthenon Centauromachy (indirect allegory, Persian Wars, civilisation vs barbarism); Bassae Amazonomachy (Greeks vs eastern ‘other’; British Museum); both placed on sacred temples for maximum authority. Roman: Augustus of Prima Porta (personal cosmic claim; divine descent through Cupid/Venus; breastplate programme); Ara Pacis (Aeneas panel linking Augustus to Trojan piety; Roma panel; fertility/peace panel). Evaluates whether the approach was effective and whether Greek indirect allegory or Roman direct personal myth-use was more powerful. Multiple named sources used. Supported conclusion.
Secure (5–6): Covers both cultures with relevant named sources; clear argument; some evaluation.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant content; limited source use; limited evaluation.
Emerging (1–2): Descriptive; sources absent or vague.

practice_questions.text: Give two mythological battles that appear in the sculpture programmes of classical temples or monuments.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: the Centauromachy (Parthenon south metopes; also at Bassae); the Amazonomachy (Bassae frieze, British Museum); the Gigantomachy (also appears on Greek temples as a battle of gods against giants, another symbol of order over chaos).

knowledge_checks.q: What battle is shown on the south metopes of the Parthenon, representing the victory of civilisation over barbarism?
The figure of Cupid riding a dolphin at the base of the Augustus of Prima Porta statue refers to which goddess?
The _____ frieze in the British Museum depicts both an Amazonomachy and a Centauromachy from the interior of a Greek temple.
The Ara Pacis includes a panel showing the Trojan hero _____ making a sacrifice, linking Augustus to Rome's divine origins.
Match each source to the political message it communicates:
right: Athenian victory over barbarism, coded as myth
Augustus as cosmically ordained ruler with divine descent
Augustus's peace as Rome's divinely destined golden age

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Centauromachy on the Parthenon south metopes represent as a mythological allegory?
flashcard_questions.a: Greek (Athenian) victory over the Persians, shown as civilisation defeating barbarism.

flashcard_questions.q: Where is the Bassae frieze now kept, and what battles does it depict?
flashcard_questions.a: The British Museum; it depicts an Amazonomachy and a Centauromachy.
Mapping mythological figures or battles onto a real political situation as a coded commentary.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the breastplate of the Augustus of Prima Porta statue show?
flashcard_questions.a: A cosmic scene: sky god (Caelus), earth goddess (Terra), the Parthians returning Roman standards, Sol and Aurora.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Ara Pacis dedicated?
What did the Amazons represent in Greek art as a political symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: The eastern barbaric ‘other’ — a society with inverted values, defeated by Greek civilised order.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Roman monument shows Aeneas sacrificing alongside a procession of the imperial family?
flashcard_questions.a: The Ara Pacis (Altar of Augustan Peace).

flashcard_questions.q: How is the political use of myth in the Parthenon different from that of the Augustus of Prima Porta?
flashcard_questions.a: The Parthenon uses indirect mythological allegory; the Prima Porta statue places the emperor personally within the divine narrative.
The mythological battle between the Lapiths and the Centaurs, symbolising civilisation defeating barbarism.
A mythological battle between Greek heroes and the Amazons, symbolising Greek victory over eastern barbarism.

glossary_terms.definition: The mythological battle between the Lapiths and the Centaurs, shown on the south metopes of the Parthenon as a symbol of the victory of civilisation over barbarism.
The practice of mapping mythological figures or stories onto a contemporary political situation, so that myth becomes a coded commentary on present events.
A mythological battle between Greek heroes and the Amazons, a race of warrior women from the east; used in Greek art as a symbol of Greek victory over eastern barbarism.

A marble statue of Augustus, the first Roman emperor, found at Prima Porta near Rome; Augustus holds a commander's baton and wears armour whose breastplate depicts the cosmos under Roman order, with a figure of Cupid at the base referencing his divine descent from Venus.

The Altar of Augustan Peace, a marble monument in Rome dedicated in 9 BC; its carved relief panels combine a solemn procession of the imperial family with mythological allegories celebrating Rome's divine destiny and the peace brought by Augustus.
